app.name: xData
app.tagline: Learn to protect your data and stay safe with AI.

course.title: Privacy and AI Safety
course.blurb: Protect your data and spot AI-powered scams. 3 weeks, 6 lessons, at your own pace.

tips: Tip: three random words make a strong password!
Tip: a real company will never rush you to pay by text.
Tip: if a video looks too shocking to be true, check who else is reporting it.
Tip: never type a card PIN or password into a chatbot.
Tip: when unsure, stop and ask someone you trust.

steps.title: Data about you
steps.text: Personal data is any information that can point to you. Tap each part to see why.

parts: An address says where to find you.
An email address is personal data too.
A photo can show your face and sometimes where it was taken.

steps.title: Some data needs extra care
steps.text: Health details, beliefs, and fingerprint or face scans are more sensitive. Misuse can do more harm, so companies must take extra care with them.

steps.title: How much are you giving away?
steps.text: Apps and websites collect data all the time. Tick what an app might ask for and watch the meter.

levels.label: Low
levels.note: Small details are usually fine, but think before sharing more.

levels.label: Medium
levels.note: Put together, these details make you easier to find and target.

levels.label: High
levels.note: That is a lot. Only share if you trust the service and really need to.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.text: Data can be sold, leaked or used by scammers. Follow the trail.

steps.title: You sign up
steps.note: You give a name, email or more.

steps.title: Company stores it
steps.note: It sits in a database you cannot see.

steps.title: It leaks or is shared
steps.note: A breach or a sale puts it in other hands.

steps.title: Scammers use it
steps.note: They write messages that seem to know you.

steps.title: You have rights
steps.text: Under UK data law you can ask a company what it holds about you, ask it to fix mistakes, and in many cases ask it to delete your data.

steps.prompt: Which piece of personal data would you find hardest to get back once it was public, and why?

steps.title: Why passwords matter
steps.text: A password is the front door to your accounts. A weak one lets anyone walk in.

steps.title: Three random words
steps.text: Long beats clever. Three random words joined together are strong and easy to remember. Try the tester. Never type a password you really use.

steps.title: What to avoid
steps.text: Guessing tools try these first. Tap to see why.

parts: Very common. Attackers try these first.
Names and years are easy to guess.
Keyboard patterns are on every guess list.

steps.title: One password per account
steps.text: If one site leaks your password, attackers try it everywhere else.

steps.title: Same password reused
steps.note: One password opens many doors.

steps.title: One site is hacked
steps.note: Your password is now in a leaked list.

steps.title: Attacker tries it elsewhere
steps.note: Email, shops and games get tested automatically.

steps.title: Many accounts taken
steps.note: A single leak becomes many.

steps.title: Add extra locks
steps.text: Turn on two-step verification, so a code or approval is needed after your password. A password manager can create and remember a different password for every account.

steps.prompt: Which account do you use most that would cause the most trouble if someone else got in? What will you change?

steps.title: Anatomy of a scam text
steps.text: Tap each highlighted part to see why it is suspicious.

parts: Sender names can be faked. Anyone can type a company name.
A strange web address that is not the company's real site.

steps.title: Common red flags
steps.text: Watch for: rushing you, asking for money or codes, odd links, messages you did not expect, and threats if you do not act.

steps.title: Check before you click
steps.text: Slow down. You can always check another way.

steps.title: Stop
steps.note: Do not tap the link or call the number in the message.

steps.title: Check another way
steps.note: Open the official app, or type the website address yourself.

steps.title: Report
steps.note: Forward scam texts to 7726 and scam emails to report@phishing.gov.uk.

steps.title: Delete
steps.note: Delete the message once you have reported it.

steps.title: Where to report
steps.text: Forward scam texts for free to 7726. Forward scam emails to report@phishing.gov.uk. If you lost money, tell your bank and report the fraud to the police.

steps.title: If you already clicked
steps.text: Do not panic or feel silly. Scams fool many people. If you entered card details, call your bank using the number on your card. Change any password you typed, and tell someone you trust.

steps.prompt: Describe a scam message you have seen, or one you think you could fall for. What gave it away?

lessons.title: Identity theft
sources: Action Fraud and bank guidance (to confirm in legal review)

steps.title: What is identity theft?
steps.text: Identity theft is when someone uses your details to open accounts, borrow money or pretend to be you.

steps.title: How thieves get details
steps.text: They collect small clues from posts, leaks and scam messages. Tap to see which clues help them.

parts: Look at my new bank card!
Never post card photos. Numbers and the security code can be used to pay.
A birthday is often used to check identity.
A name and town help someone find you.

steps.title: Warning signs
steps.text: Payments you do not recognise, post for someone you do not know, a refused application you did not expect, or accounts you never opened.

steps.title: Protect yourself
steps.text: Share less online, use strong different passwords, shred papers with your details, and check your bank statements and credit report regularly.

steps.title: If it happens to you
steps.text: Contact your bank straight away. Change your passwords and report the fraud. Keep notes of what happened and when.

steps.prompt: Which step do you think best protects against identity theft? Say what you will do differently.

steps.title: What is a deepfake?
steps.text: A deepfake is a video, image or voice made or changed by AI to look real. They can be fun, but they can also trick people.

steps.title: Voice clone scams
steps.text: Scammers can copy a voice from a short clip. A call from a 'relative' asking for money in a hurry may be fake. Agree a family safe word, and call back on a number you already know.

steps.title: Clues to look for
steps.text: No clue is perfect, and fakes keep improving. Tap each clue.

parts: Lips that do not match the words
Lip-sync glitches can be a clue.
Hair and face edges can look smudged.
AI often struggles with small details.
Content made to shock spreads fast. Pause before sharing.

steps.title: Check before you share
steps.text: Take a moment before you pass anything on.

steps.title: Pause
steps.note: Strong feelings are a signal to slow down.

steps.title: Who posted it?
steps.note: Is it a known account or a brand new one?

steps.title: Who else reports it?
steps.note: Look for trusted news sites.

steps.title: Share only if sure
steps.note: If you are not sure, do not share.

steps.title: If you are targeted
steps.text: Tell someone you trust, keep evidence, and report it to the platform. Sharing fake intimate images of someone can be a crime in the UK. Under 18? Childline (0800 1111, free) can help.

steps.prompt: Have you seen a video or voice clip that turned out to be fake? How did you find out?

lessons.title: Chatbots and your data
sources: ICO: Guidance on AI and data protection
ICO: Rights related to automated decision making

steps.title: What chatbots do with your words
steps.text: What you type may be stored, reviewed or used to improve the service. Check the privacy settings and read what the service says.

steps.title: What not to share
steps.text: Tap the parts of this message that you should not type into a chatbot.

parts: A full name is rarely needed to get help.
Name plus school makes you easy to find.
Never share PINs or passwords with a chatbot or anyone else.

steps.title: AI can be wrong
steps.text: Chatbots can sound sure and still be wrong. Check anything important.

steps.title: Ask
steps.note: Keep the question free of private details.

steps.title: Read
steps.note: Treat the answer as a draft, not a fact.

steps.title: Check
steps.note: Compare with a trusted source.

steps.title: Decide
steps.note: You make the final call.

steps.title: Your rights
steps.text: If a decision that really affects you is made only by a computer, you can often ask for a person to look at it again. The ICO website explains your rights.

steps.title: Using AI safely
steps.text: Use privacy settings, keep secrets out, check the facts, and tell someone you trust if something online feels wrong.

steps.prompt: What is one rule you will follow the next time you use an AI chatbot?

questions.prompt: Which of these is personal data?
questions.explanation: An address can lead someone to you, so it is personal data.

questions.prompt: A photo of your face can be personal data.
questions.explanation: A photo can identify you, and sometimes shows where you were.

questions.prompt: Safe or risky?
questions.text: Posting your school name and daily bus route on a public profile.
questions.explanation: Together they show strangers where you will be and when.

questions.prompt: Tap the details you should not post publicly.
questions.text: Hi! I am Alex, I live at [[22 Park Lane]], my number is [[07700 900123]] and I love football.
questions.explanation: Your address and phone number should stay private.

questions.prompt: Which password is strongest?
questions.explanation: Several random words make a long password that is hard to guess.

questions.prompt: Using the same password everywhere is fine if it is long.
questions.explanation: If one site leaks it, attackers can open all your accounts.

questions.prompt: Safe or risky?
questions.text: Sharing your password with a friend so they can play on your account.
questions.explanation: Once shared, you lose control of it. Friends can share it on.

questions.prompt: What does two-step verification add?
options: A second check, such as a code, after your password
questions.explanation: A second check stops someone who has only your password.

questions.prompt: Tap the red flags in this text message.
questions.text: URGENT: your parcel is on hold. Pay [[a £1.99 fee]] at [[parcel-redeliver.xyz]] [[within 1 hour]] or it will be returned.
questions.explanation: Pressure, a payment request and a strange link are classic scam signs.

questions.prompt: A text says your bank account is locked and tells you to tap a link. What is the best action?
options: Open your bank's official app or call the number on your card
questions.explanation: Always contact your bank through a route you already trust.

questions.prompt: Scammers can fake the sender name shown on a message.
questions.explanation: Anyone can type a company name as the sender.

questions.prompt: Safe or risky?
questions.text: Typing a website address yourself instead of tapping a link in a message.
questions.explanation: Typing it yourself avoids fake links.

questions.prompt: Which details are most useful to an identity thief?
options: Your date of birth and address
questions.explanation: Banks and companies often use these to check who you are.

questions.prompt: You only need to worry about identity theft if you are rich.
questions.explanation: Thieves use anyone's details to take out credit or open accounts.

questions.prompt: Safe or risky?
questions.text: Posting a photo of your new bank card.
questions.explanation: The card number and security code can be used to pay.

questions.prompt: You see a payment you do not recognise. What do you do first?
questions.explanation: The sooner your bank knows, the sooner it can help.

questions.prompt: A shocking video of a famous person appears. What is the first check?
options: Do trusted news sites report it?
questions.explanation: Quality and likes can be faked. Trusted reports are a better check.

questions.prompt: If a video looks very realistic, it must be real.
questions.explanation: Modern deepfakes can look very real.

questions.prompt: Safe or risky?
questions.text: Sending money after a call that sounds like your relative, without checking another way.
questions.explanation: Voices can be cloned. Call back on a number you already know.

questions.prompt: What helps protect against voice clone scams?
options: A family safe word and calling back on a known number
questions.explanation: A safe word and a call-back check out a caller.

questions.prompt: Which should you never type into a chatbot?
questions.explanation: PINs and passwords should stay private.

questions.prompt: AI chatbots are always correct.
questions.explanation: They can sound sure and still be wrong. Check important facts.

questions.prompt: Safe or risky?
questions.text: Asking a chatbot for study tips without using your real name.
questions.explanation: No private details are shared.

questions.prompt: Tap the details you should not give a chatbot.
questions.text: Hi, my name is [[Priya Shah]], I go to [[Leeds High School]] and my password is [[blue-moon-77]]. Can you help me revise?
questions.explanation: A full name, school and password are private.
